extracted.intended_audience: aspiring authors preparing query letters to literary agents
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for crafting the single stakes sentence that ends a query synopsis and convinces literary agents the story has compelling, sustainable tension. Focuses on formula, placement, common mistakes, and genre-specific emphasis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stakes sentence formula
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the exact pattern highlighted as working most often — simple, clear, and powerful. Use it to end your synopsis so agents immediately understand the central decision and cost driving the story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Place stakes sentence as final sentence of synopsis
rubrics_metrics.description: Your stakes sentence should be the final sentence of your synopsis section.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typical query structure: 1) Opening/personalization and title, word count, genre, comps; 2) Synopsis (1-2 paragraphs); 3) Stakes sentence ← the climax of your synopsis; 4) Author bio (1 paragraph).

rubrics_metrics.name: Make stakes specific and concrete
rubrics_metrics.description: Stakes must be specific rather than vague (avoid abstracts like 'love vs duty').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article gives the bad example 'Sarah must choose between love and duty' and the good example 'Sarah must decide if marrying for love is worth losing her inheritance and disappointing her dying mother' — specificity adds vividness and helps readers care.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show agency — include a clear decision point
rubrics_metrics.description: Stakes require agency: the protagonist must decide/choose and risk something, not merely react to events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the protagonist is only reacting, the stakes aren't working. Agents want characters with power and real decision-making in complicated circumstances (but not so complicated they can't be described in a query).

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify the protagonist's goal
rubrics_metrics.description: Step 1 in crafting stakes: state what your main character wants more than anything.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'CHARACTER A wants to go to art camp', 'CHARACTER B wants to know the truth about her adoption', 'CHARACTER C wants to contain the supernatural threat.' This frames the choice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Name the obstacle
rubrics_metrics.description: Step 2: name what's standing in the protagonist's way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'CHARACTER A’s family disapproves of him going to art camp', 'CHARACTER B’s grandmother might be hiding dangerous secrets', 'CHARACTER C’s past trauma is tied to the current crisis.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Define the cost (what they'll lose)
rubrics_metrics.description: Step 3: state what the protagonist will lose if they pursue their goal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'CHARACTER A risks family relationships and approval and the camp prize money', 'CHARACTER B risks her safety and relationships', 'CHARACTER C must face painful memories.' Make the cost concrete and consequential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combine elements into one stakes sentence
rubrics_metrics.description: Step 4: fuse protagonist, obstacle/choice, and cost into the formula sentence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the formula exactly: '[Character] must decide if [choice/action] is worth [consequence/risk]'. Keep it tight and positioned as the synopsis climax.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid withholding information
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not leave agents wondering by being elliptical or vague about the conflict ('Eventually, I make peace').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bad: 'Eventually, I make peace' — leaves readers asking how and why. Better: 'I must make peace with grief as a permanent companion.' Be explicit about what you mean and the angle of the story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid too much setup and condense backstory/worldbuilding
rubrics_metrics.description: Don’t spend multiple paragraphs on backstory or worldbuilding before stating the stakes; condense setup to focus on plot and the protagonist's choice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a query buries the plot under exposition, agents advise condensing the setup to leave space for the stakes sentence. The masterclass recommended giving more coverage to plot and compressing early background where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid vague stakes phrasing
rubrics_metrics.description: Phrases like 'She must find her way forward' or 'He must learn what really matters' are insufficiently descriptive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Replace vague phrasings with concrete, risky consequences and choices — example: 'She must choose between accepting her best friend’s death as an accident or investigating the evidence that suggests murder—risking her own safety and destroying her friend’s reputation.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Stakes should be emotionally charged and compelling
rubrics_metrics.description: Stakes must be clear, emotionally charged, and make the reader care even without full context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Queries that catch agents' attention end with 'clear, emotionally charged stakes' — not implied or 'wait and see' stakes. Make the choice emotionally resonant so agents want to read the manuscript.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure the stakes can sustain the novel's length (sufficient tension)
rubrics_metrics.description: Agents assess whether the central tension is strong enough to carry the projected word count (e.g., 48K, 60K).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask whether the tension of the project is enough to sustain a full-length book. If not, rethink the stakes or structure so the central decision will support the manuscript.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjust stakes emphasis by genre
rubrics_metrics.description: The formula holds across genres but the emphasis shifts: internal conflict for literary, relationship growth for romance, physical danger and truth for mystery/thriller, and both personal and world-level stakes for fantasy/SF.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples provided: Literary — expose moral/psychological cost; Romance — balance personal growth and relationship risk; Thriller — highlight danger and moral compromises; Fantasy/SF — include consequences for the broader world as well as the protagonist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Testing checklist for your stakes sentence
rubrics_metrics.description: Four questions to self-test the stakes sentence: Is it specific? Is it compelling? Is it clear? Does it show enough tension to carry a full novel?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical test: have someone who hasn't read the manuscript read only your query for 60 seconds, then ask whether they can state exactly what the protagonist must decide and what they might lose. If yes, you're ready to query; if not, revise.
